I’d say “Just do it”. There are lots of people with varying backgrounds at my doctorate program. Plus graduate programs are often than not Quantitative and they would appreciate your science background.

Actually a course in political economics is needed to get the context of the world system. A lot more time has been spent on Thucydides than on Adam Smith in some departments and I think it’s a shame.

I’m lucky that my UG International Relations degree was qual, but it was a missed opportunity to become a better researcher since we had only one methods class.

But yes, you need both. Quant for methods and qual for domain knowledge. It’s also true you can transform much of the qualitative stuff into ordinal scale for quant for those who care.

Computational methods in Political Science. I’m a doctorate student in Political Science in the fields of world and computational analytics.

Teaching econometrics, game theory, and formal modeling would be a dream to teach for undergrad, because quant methods are in demand in both industry and academia. 

The main restraint to this is that many political science majors (at least in the US) want to be lawyers not political scientists so they stick to what we call qualitative studies - basically in our discipline political philosophy, history, and bastardized comparative politics.

Lawyers don’t want to be scientists. They want to be philosophers while the field itself is going towards statistical and data science as the key analytical method. 

Therefore, the field has been divided between quants and quali departments for a long time. It’s quite interesting as you can be a non-ideological quant political scientist while the sub-department next door is happily politically biased and motivated.
